transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Janine Herst.
A leaked U.S. intelligence memo is raising questions about limits on military cooperation
with Canada.
Julian Abraham has more.
The leaked Classified Department of Defense memo first reported by The Washington Post
has dominated conversations at the Halifax International Security Forum.
Republican South Dakota Senator Mike Rounds confirmed its existence in a speech at the
forum.
While it was a classified discussion, it was one that was put together several months ago,
only recently signed, and then it was unfortunately then released publicly.
Rounds says, according to the memo, U.S. military officials will need permission to attend Canadian
think-tank events or social gatherings, the latest strain on an already fraught relationship
between the two allies.
But speaking at the forum, Canada's Defense Minister David McGinty insisted cooperation
with the U.S. on defense, security and intelligence continues.
For NPR News, I'm Julian Abraham in Halifax.
The U.N. says there have been more Israeli settler attacks on the Palestinian olive harvest
this year than in any year since record-keeping began, and it's calling on Israel to urgently
act to protect harvesters.
NPR's Lauren Freire reports.
The United Nations cites more than 400 Israeli settler attacks since September on Palestinian
olive farmers, as well as activists, journalists and diplomats who try to help them.
And it says more than 55,000 pounds of produce have been vandalized or stolen.
This weekend, a Palestinian lawmaker in Israel's parliament shared video he says shows Israeli
settlers stealing fruit and vegetables from Palestinian vendors in the occupied West Bank.
Accusing settlers who serve in Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's far-right government
of allowing them to do so.
The Israeli military has said it seeks to prevent friction during the olive harvest.
But the U.N. accuses it of, quote, "acquiescence, support and participation in attacks."
Lauren Freire, NPR News, Tel Aviv.
In California, where high tides and heavy rains are forecast, one mayor is urging residents
to change their Thanksgiving plans, and here's Ava Berger reports.
As Americans set their minds on pumpkin pie and cranberry sauce, the weather is not cooperating.
San Francisco Mayor Daniel Laurie said next week the city is expecting extreme high tides
and rain.
I'm going to ask you all to consider not traveling unless it is absolutely essential starting
Monday afternoon and going into Wednesday afternoon.
Two atmospheric rivers, which are long bands of water vapor that dump rain on certain areas,
will hover over Northern California and the Pacific Northwest.
On the eastern seaboard, a storm is forecasted to move through the Carolinas into New England.
Meteorologists say during a busy travel week, any challenging weather can cause delays.
Ava Berger, NPR News.
And about 81 million people are expected to travel for Thanksgiving.
This is NPR.
Scientists have discovered a tiny area in the brain that appears to act as a link between
hearing and speaking.
John Hamilton has more on research in the journal Science.
It's called Wernicke's area, and for more than a century, it's been known as a place
where the brain processes incoming words.
But Dr. Eddie Chang of the University of California San Francisco says a study of 28 people found
Wernicke's area has another role.
In addition to the listening function, it also has a function for planning the words
that we're about to say next.
Just before a person speaks, a small group of neurons in Wernicke's area begin sending
signals that help organize the impending string of syllables.
The discovery of neurons involved in both input and output could help explain how children
learn to say the words they hear.
For NPR News, I'm John Hamilton.
In California, mountain lions in Los Angeles are getting their own crossing bridge to help
them safely get to the other side and avoid cars.
This bridge officially opens next month, and it will let the animals walk high above the
101 freeway into the Santa Monica Mountains.
Beth Pratt is president of Wildlife Crossing Fund.
This is part of a path where wildlife can literally have a safe passageway from the
Pacific Ocean to the Sierra.
It's pretty amazing.
She says wildlife crossings are up to 97 percent effective in saving animals' lives, and some
animals are already using it; remote cameras have captured coyotes using that corridor.
I'm Janine Herft, NPR News, in Washington.
This message comes from Schwab.

all in one place.
No matter your investing goal, life stage, amount to invest, or know-how, you can invest

topics.text: Leaked Pentagon memo restricts U.S. military contact with Canadian think tanks, sparking alliance tensions
U.N. reports record Israeli settler attacks on Palestinian olive harvest, calls on Israel to act
San Francisco mayor urges residents to avoid travel as atmospheric rivers and high tides approach
Scientists find brain area Wernicke's region also helps plan words before speaking, study shows
Los Angeles opens wildlife crossing bridge over 101 Freeway for mountain lions next month
